evidence: pyproject.toml:10 requires-python >=3.11. asyncio.timeout was added in 3.11 (documented API). On deadline expiry the context manager cancels the task, and its __aexit__ converts the resulting CancelledError into builtin TimeoutError (3.11 and 3.12), so the 'except TimeoutError' at sql_threads.py:158 catches it. The slot.acquire() at line 157 is inside the async with at line 156. Based on CPython documented behavior, not a run. An external cancellation, as opposed to the timeout's own, still propagates as CancelledError, which is intended.

sql_threads.py:155-163 wraps `await slot.acquire()` in asyncio.timeout and catches only TimeoutError. Based on my recollection of CPython 3.11/3.12 (I did not read the CPython source in this run): a cancel arriving after the slot future was resolved makes task.cancel() set _must_cancel, so CancelledError is thrown at the `await fut` inside Semaphore.acquire. acquire's except-CancelledError branch gives the slot back (value += 1, wake next) and re-raises, so the slot is accounted for. Timeout.__aexit__ converts to TimeoutError only when the state is EXPIRING and uncancel() <= the cancelling count captured on entry. With an external cancel the count is higher, and with no expiry the state is plain ENTERED, so CancelledError propagates unchanged. SqlWorkersBusyError is therefore not raised (line 163 sits only in the except TimeoutError branch).

sql_threads.py:164-174: after `await slot.acquire()` returns (line 157/165), there is no await before `_get_executor().submit(call)` at 169, so a task cancellation cannot be delivered in that window. A cancel at the acquire await itself is handled by asyncio.Semaphore.acquire, which returns the slot if it was granted. Any BaseException from submit (including a KeyboardInterrupt-like or executor-shutdown error) is caught at 170-172 and calls slot.release() before re-raising. After a successful submit, the done callback at 174 releases the slot via _release_slot. Every exit path therefore returns the slot. The rejection line concerns the MySQL docstring and does not affect this claim.

sql_threads.py:115-125 catches RuntimeError from loop.call_soon_threadsafe and checks loop.is_closed(). In CPython BaseEventLoop.call_soon_threadsafe calls _check_closed(), which raises RuntimeError('Event loop is closed'), and is_closed() just returns the self._closed flag, with no lock or thread affinity. So it is safe from a worker thread. A closed loop returns silently. Any other RuntimeError reaches the error log. This is from my knowledge of CPython; I did not read the stdlib source in this environment. The rejection line concerns the MySQL docstring and does not apply.

sql_threads.py:115-125: _release_slot catches only RuntimeError around loop.call_soon_threadsafe(slot.release). A slot.release error runs later inside the loop, not in _release_slot, so that half of the claim holds. A non-RuntimeError from call_soon_threadsafe is not caught and would propagate out of _release_slot, so the claim's literal wording is false there. concurrent.futures Future._invoke_callbacks catches Exception and logs it, so it would not crash the pool. I found no shipped caller or documented state that produces such an exception with the stdlib loop, and no requirement that _release_slot must never raise. Rejection line concerns the MySQL runner docstring and does not cover this claim.

sql_threads.py:147-176. Waiting uses asyncio.timeout around slot.acquire() (156-157), not wait_for. A cancellation in the same tick as a grant makes Semaphore.acquire raise CancelledError and hand the slot back, so the call never reaches submit. Between acquire returning (157/165) and submit (169) there is no await, so no cancellation can be delivered there. Cancellation only lands at line 176, after submit, which is a started call and outside the claim. A timeout that fires in the same tick as a grant also surfaces as CancelledError inside acquire, which returns the slot, and is then converted to SqlWorkersBusyError, so the call still does not run. Not exhaustively verified against every CPython Semaphore version; I relied on the 3.11+ semantics that asyncio.timeout requires. The rejection concerns the MySQL runner docstring and does not touch this claim.

sql_threads.py:86 _slots is a per-loop WeakKeyDictionary; lines 148-150 create a Semaphore(8) per loop. The executor (line 92-99) is a single process-wide ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8). Two concurrent loops can each hold 8 slots, so up to 16 calls get past acquire. Calls beyond 8 are queued inside ThreadPoolExecutor.submit (line 169) after the slot is acquired. The wait timeout (156) and _warn_saturated (152) are only reached when slot.locked() for that loop's own semaphore, so they do not apply to the executor queue. Absolute-claim input traced: two loops each submitting 8 blocking calls at once. Each loop's semaphore is not locked, so none warns or times out, and 8 calls sit in the executor queue. The rejection about MySQL run_sql does not concern this claim.
